title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
authors: Ruben Ortiz Cordero, Gaven K. Smart, Harshada Gothankar, Emilio Supsupin, Priya Bhosale, Mayur Virarkar
abstract: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum machine learning is being explored for medical imaging, but current evidence is largely limited to small-scale hybrid quantum-classical demonstrations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Practical value depends on efficient data encoding, quantum algorithms, and measurement strategies—not superposition alone.
method: Reviews core quantum concepts and superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware.
Surveys quantum support vector machines, neural networks, variational circuits, and convolutional networks.
Introduces FRQI and NEQR image representations and summarizes radiology applications.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nearly all surveyed systems use hybrid pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators rather than clinical deployments.
infographic.watch_item: Noise and data-loading overhead constrain current hardware; clinical feasibility and practical quantum advantage remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists

title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
authors: Saverio Monaco, Jamal Slim, Ran Xue, Dirk Krücker, Kerstin Borras
abstract: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

infographic.key_insight: Pauli propagation enables classical pre-training of large, shallow parametrized quantum circuits while leaving target states or samples classically intractable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Classical pre-training reduces reliance on costly quantum gradient estimation and supplies parameters ready for deployment on quantum hardware.
method: Propagate observables backward through the circuit to derive a parametric loss expression.
Use weight- and degree-based truncation plus pruning to control propagation cost.
Optimize parameters classically, then deploy the trained circuits on quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 64-qubit demonstrations for a two-dimensional Ising VQE and binary-image generation, with pre-trained parameters deployed on IBM's ibm_berlin processor.
infographic.watch_item: Truncation and pruning make propagation tractable but require checking approximation error and its effect on hardware performance.
infographic.paper_title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware

title: Quantum Anomaly Detection in network traffic using Variational Quantum Classifiers
authors: Mir H M Ilham, Hardique Dasore, Abdulrahman Ababneh, Hafidz A Kabira, Samyam Shrestha, Jeyasri Sundar
abstract: The increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape requires more advanced network anomaly detection systems. Although, classical machine learning models are known to be effective, they reach computational bottlenecks when processing high-dimensional data. This study investigates the potential of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) for network traffic anomaly detection by evaluating four distinct Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) architectures. A synthetic network traffic dataset is generated for the evaluations. The VQC models systematically varied feature encoding methods, parameterized ansatz circuits, quantum neural network types, and classical optimizers. Experimental results show that a trade-off exists between circuit expressivity and optimization stability. Deeper circuits (VQC-4) achieved higher accuracy of upto 89.0\%, while simultaneously being sensitive to training conditions. A shallower variant (VQC-1) under performed, although it had consistent and stable optimization curves. Class-dependent biases were also observed such as in VQC-2, where the model struggled to find an effective decision boundary, and produced a large number of false negatives. The best performing model in this study (VQC-3) combined ZFeatureMap with RealAmplitudes ansatz, optimized using ADAM. Comparative analysis against classical machine learning models such as Support Vector Machine and Random Forest reveal a performance gap, where classical models are able to achieve perfect classification performance on the synthetic data. It is concluded that classical algorithms remain dominant in their ability to classify structured data with relatively simple class separations. However, due to the observed potential of certain VQC configurations to learn decision boundaries to classify data, their utility for future applications in noisier, higher-dimensional problems is highlighted.

infographic.key_insight: Variational quantum classifiers showed an expressivity–stability trade-off in network anomaly detection, but classical models performed better on the synthetic data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Feature encoding, circuit architecture, and optimizer selection matter for quantum anomaly detectors, while classical methods remain the stronger baseline for this task.
method: Generated synthetic network traffic data.
Evaluated four VQC architectures with different encodings, ansatz circuits, quantum neural network types, and optimizers.
Compared VQCs against Support Vector Machine and Random Forest models.
infographic.evidence_signal: VQC-4 reached up to 89.0% accuracy, VQC-3 was identified as best overall using ZFeatureMap, RealAmplitudes, and ADAM, and classical baselines achieved perfect classification on the synthetic data.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic data with relatively simple class separations does not establish real-world effectiveness or quantum advantage on noisy, high-dimensional traffic.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Anomaly Detection in network traffic using Variational Quantum Classifiers

title: $κ$-Parametrized Boltzmann Distribution Sampling on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: João Marcos Cavalcanti de Albuquerque Neto, Gustavo Castro do Amaral, Guilherme Penello Temporão
abstract: Generative models use training data to produce new samples that resemble the original, with applications in classification and recommendation systems. Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are at the core of generative models but suffer from the computational intractability of training, which relies on sampling an unknown Boltzmann Distribution (BD). The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can assist RBM training, potentially providing benefits over strictly classical strategies. One particular problem is determining the quantum circuit depth for an arbitrary problem size that yields the expected sampling results. In this study, we evaluate QAOA-assisted sampling of BDs using Qiskit's Aer Simulator by analysing the inverse effective temperature of the distribution, $κ$, for tractable problem sizes. The results provide numerical evidence, based on Qiskit Aer simulations, that parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA (PAQ-QAOA) can approximate RBM Boltzmann sampling for the tractable instances considered, while hardware performance and scaling remain open questions.

infographic.key_insight: Simulations suggest parameterized annealing-scheduled QAOA (PAQ-QAOA) can approximate the Boltzmann sampling needed for restricted Boltzmann machine training on tractable instances.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QAOA-assisted sampling could support quantum-enhanced generative-model training, but practical benefits over classical sampling remain unproven.
method: Simulate PAQ-QAOA circuits with Qiskit Aer.
Analyze sampled distributions through inverse effective temperature κ.
Evaluate Boltzmann sampling for tractable RBM problem sizes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical evidence from Qiskit Aer simulations supporting approximate RBM Boltzmann sampling for the tractable instances considered.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware performance, scaling, and circuit-depth requirements for larger problems remain open questions.
infographic.paper_title: $κ$-Parametrized Boltzmann Distribution Sampling on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
authors: Dayu Li, Naibin Zhou, Zhiyuan Chen, Zihua Chen, Yu Xu, Yuan Li
abstract: Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid control framework uses frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) to share microwave lines across superconducting qubits, targeting a 10–100× reduction in control-line count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared control lines could ease dilution-refrigerator wiring and cooling constraints on the path to large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Combine polychromatic microwave pulses with band-pass filters to multiplex gate control.
Demonstrate parallel FDM-controlled CZ and XY(π/2) gates with 1:4 multiplexing.
Integrate the gate-control scheme with on-chip DC sources in a periodically extensible architecture.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 1:4 demonstration reports average parallel-gate errors of (6.4±0.2)×10⁻³ for CZ and (10.6±0.2)×10⁻⁴ for XY(π/2), with no statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation.
infographic.watch_item: The projected 10–100× line reduction remains to be validated at scale, where frequency allocation, filter integration, and crosstalk may constrain performance.
infographic.paper_title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing

title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems
authors: Zhi-Yao Ning, Zi-Xiang Li, Naoki Kawashima
abstract: We construct a controllable imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems using spatially modulated local rotations without changing initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes. This feature unambiguously isolates the redistribution of spectral weights as the sole driver of the anomalous relaxation. Using the compact-boson description, we reveal that these twists act as precise mode selectors: higher-harmonic twists exclusively populate high-energy standing waves, structurally bypassing slow-decaying infrared modes to accelerate convergence. We derive exact analytical crossing times for these reversals and demonstrate that intentionally reintroducing the slow-mode population systematically delays the ITME. This exact mechanism is validated beyond the fixed-point theory via calculations on interacting XXZ chains and ladders. Furthermore, a twelve-qubit simulation of variational quantum imaginary-time evolution reproduces the reversals and their controlled delay, providing a concrete route to realize this protocol in realistic quantum circuits. Ultimately, these results provide a strictly controllable and exact starting point for realizing and investigating the imaginary-time Mpemba effect, establishing a foundational paradigm to harness anomalous non-equilibrium relaxation in quantum ground-state preparations.

infographic.key_insight: Spatially patterned spin rotations control the imaginary-time Mpemba effect by redistributing spectral weight away from slow modes while preserving initial bipartite entanglement spectra and correlation magnitudes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Twist-designed initial states offer a route to faster quantum ground-state preparation by selectively avoiding slowly decaying excitations.
method: Apply spatially modulated local rotations to tune initial-state spectral weights.
Use compact-boson theory to identify mode selection and derive exact crossing times.
Test interacting XXZ chains and ladders and simulate variational imaginary-time evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation in interacting XXZ systems and a twelve-qubit variational simulation reproducing relaxation reversals and their controlled delay.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware robustness and scaling beyond the twelve-qubit simulation remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Twist-controlled imaginary-time Mpemba effect in quantum spin systems

title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
authors: Benjamin Rossdeutscher, Jingbo Wang
abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: A gate-level NV-QWOA implementation amplifies optimal and near-optimal solutions to the Closest String problem without instance-specific parameter optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The automated circuit workflow and analytical resource estimates provide a basis for quantum hardware experiments and classical benchmarking.
method: Encode candidate strings and evaluate their maximum Hamming distance to the reference strings.
Apply non-variational quantum-walk optimization using a problem-size-dependent phase parameter to mitigate excessive phase wrapping.
Compile into one- and two-qubit gates, with O(nm log k) qubits and O(pm log² n + pn log n) circuit depth.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplified optimal and near-optimal candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation-based amplification does not establish practical quantum advantage; hardware performance and comparisons with classical algorithms remain to be evaluated.
infographic.paper_title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA

title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes
authors: Vicenzo Scavino Alfaro
abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is usually validated by the accuracy of mitigated observables, yet variational quantum optimization uses those observables to select parameters. We ask whether, and by how much, an accuracy gain from ZNE coincides with a worse decision. In depth-one simulations of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut on four to six qubits, each sampled $120\times120$ landscape yields both its mean-squared error (MSE) and the ideal regret of its selected grid minimum, comparing Richardson orders one to three with unmitigated estimation at the same total shot budget per grid point. In an exploratory screen of 675 conditions, whose per-point random seeds collide, a familywise (Holm) analysis retains only four of 540 replication conditions as showing both directional MSE improvement and regret increase. A frozen confirmation with 100 fresh paired repetitions per condition reproduces all four: median MSE improvements of 7.65-73.09% accompany median normalized regret increases of only 0.0031-0.0073. We distinguish a bias route, in which residual bias reorders the mean landscape, from a variance route, in which Richardson weights amplify finite-shot noise. Exact first and second moments on a bounded control grid find no bias-route reversal: mitigated mean landscapes preserve the ideal minima, and ZNE can more than halve expected MSE, yet finite-shot selections incur higher mean regret. Decision losses that survive strict testing are few and small in this benchmark, but reproducible and not revealed by aggregate MSE. We present a paired benchmark and recommend reporting decision regret alongside estimation error when mitigation is assessed for optimization. Results concern simulated exhaustive grids, not hardware or optimizer loops.

infographic.key_insight: Zero-noise extrapolation can improve QAOA landscape accuracy while slightly worsening parameter selection, so lower estimation error does not guarantee better optimization decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Validate mitigation with decision regret alongside mean-squared error under matched total shot budgets.
method: Simulate depth-one QAOA for MaxCut on 4–6 qubits using exhaustive 120×120 parameter grids.
Compare Richardson extrapolation orders 1–3 against unmitigated estimation at equal shot budgets.
Use paired repetitions and exact-moment controls to distinguish residual-bias effects from finite-shot noise amplification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four of 540 replication conditions survived Holm correction and all four reproduced in 100 fresh paired repetitions each, with median MSE improvements of 7.65–73.09% but small median normalized regret increases of 0.0031–0.0073.
infographic.watch_item: The exploratory screen had colliding per-point seeds, and findings are limited to simulated exhaustive grids—not hardware or optimizer loops.
infographic.paper_title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes

title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
authors: V. M. Tkachuk, M. I. Samar
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum-classical method for reconstructing energy-level degeneracies and thermodynamic properties of spin systems. A single ancilla qubit is used to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures. For spectra lying on a known equally spaced energy grid, the inverse discrete Fourier transform allows exact reconstruction of degeneracies in the absence of noise, without spectral leakage. The quantum circuits are optimized using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering. We demonstrate the method for frustrated Ising antiferromagnets on periodic Kagome graphs with up to 36 spins, using the ibm_kingston quantum processor. Despite substantial circuit depth and hardware noise, the reconstructed spectra retain their dominant features, and the calculated heat capacities reproduce the main temperature dependence of the exact results. Keywords: partition function, imaginary temperature, Ising model, heat capacity, ancilla qubit, quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid quantum-classical method reconstructs spin-system energy degeneracies from imaginary-temperature partition functions measured with a single ancilla qubit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables quantum-assisted thermodynamic calculations, with circuit optimizations tailored to commuting spin interactions.
method: Measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures using one ancilla qubit.
Apply an inverse discrete Fourier transform on a known, equally spaced energy grid to recover degeneracies.
Optimize circuits using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on periodic Kagome Ising antiferromagnets with up to 36 spins on ibm_kingston retained dominant spectral features and reproduced the main temperature dependence of exact heat capacities.
infographic.watch_item: Exact reconstruction requires a known, equally spaced energy grid and noiseless measurements; substantial circuit depth and hardware noise limit practical accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems

title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
authors: Timur Javid, Brian Doolittle, Colin P. Lualdi, Brittany Conner, Michael Vayninger, Eric Chitambar
abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.

infographic.key_insight: Variational optimization can compensate for imperfect optical hardware, achieving automated polarization compensation comparable to conventional methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Parameterized protocol optimization offers a practical route to calibrating noisy polarization-qubit hardware for quantum network nodes.
method: Parameterize prepare-and-measure protocols for variational optimization.
Optimize protocols experimentally on an optical testbed.
Compare gradient estimation methods and assess hardware imperfections and dark counts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a proof-of-principle optical demonstration with polarization compensation comparable to conventional methods, but provides no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on deployed fiber networks remains un demonstrated, and hardware imperfections and dark counts can affect optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
authors: Chayan Patra, Prayas Ghosh, Adwait Patkhedkar, Rahul Maitra
abstract: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed quantum-centric supercomputing combines fragment-level quantum calculations with generative learning to reconstruct molecular solutions at lower computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Splitting electronic-structure problems into parallel subsystems reduces qubit requirements, circuit depth, sampling budgets, and classical diagonalization demands.
method: Solve molecular fragments with physics-informed generative sample-based quantum diagonalization (PIGen-SQD).
Optimize local-to-global bit assignments to assemble a mapped tensor product state.
Use a second generative module to identify dominant global configurations and recover inter-fragment correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: For water and formamide dimers, the abstract reports up to 95% smaller diagonalization dimensions and an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy accuracy over conventional SQD; a 120-qubit water hexamer was split into six 20-qubit subsystems with excellent agreement with classical references.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on recovering cross-fragment correlations; the hexamer demonstration uses a dimeric approximation whose reliability for more strongly coupled systems remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions

title: Decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification for quantum low-density parity-check codes
authors: Josu Etxezarreta Martinez, Francisco Garcia-Herrero, Ruben M. Otxoa, Reza Dastbasteh
abstract: Real-time decoding is a fundamental necessity for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In this work, we introduce decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification (DAWG), an ensemble based approach that combines Tanner graph sparsification with ensembling belief-propagation (BP) decoders. The DAWG decoder runs BP decoders over the full detector error model Tanner graph for certain iterations to then transfer the posteriors to a sparsified graph in which additional rounds of BP are run. Each of the decoders in the ensemble uses a different transfer matrix to map the posterior information to the sparsified graph. We use the serial schedule for the minimum-sum BP decoders and, thus, employ Vibe decoding ideas by randomizing the schedules of each of them. The performance of the DAWG decoder is then numerically studied for bivariate bicycle codes and superdense color code circuits to be compared with other state-of-the-art decoding approaches. Importantly, the DAWG decoder shows a similar performance to Relay belief-propagation and Vibe decoding when combined with an order-$0$ Localized Statistics Decoding (LSD-$0$) post-processor. Crucially, the post-processor is called an order of magnitude less times than for Vibe with the same ensemble size, indicating that the introduced latency tail will be minimal. Furthermore, LSD-$0$ operates on a sparsified decoding graph of a fraction of the size of the full detector error model, which simplifies the resources required by specialized hardware to support it. Overall, the DAWG+LSD-$0$ decoder represents a viable low-cost BP-based decoding algorithm for quantum error correction codes.

infographic.key_insight: DAWG combines belief-propagation ensembles with weighted graph sparsification to maintain competitive quantum error-correction decoding performance while reducing post-processing demand.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Less frequent post-processing on a smaller decoding graph could reduce latency tails and specialized hardware resource requirements.
method: Run serial minimum-sum belief propagation on the full detector error model Tanner graph.
Transfer posterior information to a sparsified graph using ensemble-specific transfer matrices, then continue decoding.
Randomize ensemble schedules and apply order-0 Localized Statistics Decoding (LSD-0) as a post-processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies on bivariate bicycle codes and superdense color code circuits report DAWG+LSD-0 performance similar to Relay BP and Vibe, with roughly tenfold fewer post-processor calls than Vibe at the same ensemble size.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time latency and hardware resource savings remain to be demonstrated beyond the reported numerical evaluations.
infographic.paper_title: Decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification for quantum low-density parity-check codes

title: Fully quantum training of parametric circuits with Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
authors: Marco Burato, Leonardo Banchi
abstract: Parametric quantum circuits are usually trained by classical, local optimizers, which use the quantum computer only to evaluate the cost function, or its gradient, one point at a time. Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) takes a different route: in this quantum algorithm for continuous optimization, the parameters become the position of a quantum particle, with the cost function as its potential, and two time schedules control kinetic and potential energy so that the wavefunction explores the whole landscape and tunnels towards the global minimum. QHD, however, assumes a classically computable cost function, and its digital implementation is poorly understood: standard error bounds grow exponentially with the number of qubits per parameter, and the schedules are borrowed from classical optimization. Here we propose to train parametric circuits with QHD entirely on the quantum computer, through an online step in which the qubits encoding the parameters coherently control the circuit on a second register. We prove that, for cost functions with a smooth periodic extension, including those of parametric circuits, the simulation error admits a bound independent of the grid resolution, and that for circuits the bound grows at most linearly with the number of parameters. We also show that the ideal dynamics depends on the two schedules only through a single curve, which controls the adiabaticity of the search, and that the remaining freedom can be used to minimize the gate count. Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show that, at equal cost, schedules designed in this way markedly increase the probability of finding the global minimum.

infographic.key_insight: Fully quantum Quantum Hamiltonian Descent trains parametric circuits by encoding parameters in a quantum wavefunction that explores the cost landscape and can tunnel toward global minima.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Grid-resolution-independent simulation error bounds and gate-count-aware schedules offer a principled route to implementing quantum circuit training.
method: Use parameter-register qubits to coherently control a circuit on a second register.
Evolve parameters under kinetic and cost-potential terms with tunable schedules.
Reduce schedule design to one curve governing adiabaticity and use remaining freedom to minimize gate count.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show markedly higher global-minimum success probabilities at equal cost with the proposed schedules.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is simulation-based; practical performance under hardware noise and coherent-control overhead remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Fully quantum training of parametric circuits with Quantum Hamiltonian Descent

title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Xiantao Li
abstract: Discrete nonlinear dynamical systems arise in population models, iterative optimization, and numerical simulations, where computing many iterations can be costly in high dimensions. We study Carleman embedding for forced quadratic discrete systems and its application to quantum state preparation. Under explicit stability and initial-state assumptions, we prove that the truncation error decreases geometrically with the embedding degree, uniformly over all iterations. A central obstacle in discrete time is that the lifted update can become dense even when the original coefficient maps are sparse. We overcome this obstacle by constructing an exact auxiliary linear-system representation that applies the coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time, with row and column sparsities bounded independently of the truncation degree. After rescaling, the associated history system has a condition number that grows linearly with the iteration count, uniformly in the truncation degree. These results yield a quantum algorithm for preparing an approximation to the normalized $n$th iterate with constant success probability. Under coherent input-access assumptions, and for fixed sparsity, stability parameters, and a known positive lower bound on the final-state norm, the oracle query complexity is linear in $n$ and polylogarithmic in the inverse accuracy. Numerical experiments in one and three dimensions illustrate the convergence of the truncated embedding.

infographic.key_insight: An exact sparse auxiliary representation makes Carleman embeddings practical for quantum state preparation, with truncation error decreasing geometrically and uniformly over all iterations under stated assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For qualifying nonlinear discrete models, the approach supports quantum preparation of a normalized iterate with query complexity linear in iteration count and polylogarithmic in inverse accuracy.
method: Embed forced quadratic dynamics into a truncated linear system using tensor powers.
Apply coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time, keeping row and column sparsities bounded independently of truncation degree.
Rescale the history system to obtain condition-number growth linear in iteration count, then prepare the normalized final iterate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper proves error, sparsity, conditioning, and query-complexity bounds; numerical experiments in one and three dimensions illustrate truncation convergence.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require explicit stability and initial-state assumptions, coherent input access, fixed sparsity parameters, and a known positive lower bound on the final-state norm.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems

title: Efficient Block Encodings of Vibrational Hamiltonians
authors: Shashank G. Mehendale, Ignacio Loaiza, Shreyas Malpathak, Stepan Fomichev, Danial Motlagh, Artur F. Izmaylov
abstract: Simulation of molecular vibrations is emerging as a promising application of quantum computing in quantum chemistry. In this work, we develop new strategies for block-encoding the second-quantized $n$-mode representation of the vibrational Hamiltonian, whose algebraic structure closely parallels that of the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. We derive linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) representations of this Hamiltonian based on Pauli decomposition and tensor hypercontraction (THC) and construct efficient circuits for the corresponding block encodings. We also extend the Block-Invariant Symmetry Shift (BLISS) technique to vibrational Hamiltonians, yielding a lower LCU 1-norm and, consequently, a lower overall circuit cost. For the molecules considered here, BLISS-THC reduces the Toffoli cost of quantum phase estimation by more than two orders of magnitude relative to existing block-encoding approaches. In comparison with recent Trotter-based methods, it shows up to a ninefold reduction in the T-gate count, with the relative savings tending to increase with system size. Asymptotically, and up to polylogarithmic factors, both the Pauli and THC LCUs trade additional ancillas for a quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modes, while THC provides an additional quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modals. These results highlight the importance of Hamiltonian factorizations and Toffoli-qubit tradeoffs for reducing the computational cost of quantum simulations of molecular vibrations.

infographic.key_insight: Combining tensor hypercontraction (THC) with Block-Invariant Symmetry Shift (BLISS) substantially reduces the quantum circuit cost of simulating molecular vibrations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More efficient Hamiltonian block encodings can lower quantum phase estimation costs, while trading additional ancilla qubits for improved scaling.
method: Construct Pauli- and THC-based linear-combination-of-unitaries block encodings of second-quantized vibrational Hamiltonians.
Extend BLISS to vibrational Hamiltonians to reduce the LCU 1-norm.
Design circuits exploiting Hamiltonian factorization and Toffoli–qubit tradeoffs.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the molecules studied, BLISS-THC reduces phase-estimation Toffoli costs by more than 100× versus existing block encodings and T-gate counts by up to 9× versus recent Trotter-based methods.
infographic.watch_item: Improved scaling requires additional ancilla qubits, and the reported savings may vary with molecular system and implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Block Encodings of Vibrational Hamiltonians

title: Minimal ancilla for boosting type-I photonic fusion
authors: A. A. Melkozerov, S. S. Straupe, M. Yu. Saygin
abstract: Fusion gates enable the creation of large entangled photonic states for linear-optical quantum computing and communication protocols. However, their success probability is limited to $1/2$ without additional photonic resources. Previous schemes for boosting type-I fusion have used four ancillary single photons or a two-qubit Bell state, whose preparation is probabilistic and resource intensive. Here we propose a boosted type-I fusion gate using only two independent ancillary single photons and no entangled ancillary input. It achieves a direct success probability of $5/8$, matching that of the previous four-single-photon proposal while using half as many ancillary photons. The circuit is predominantly passive, with a single active element that applies a phase shift or swaps two modes according to intermediate photodetection outcomes. Unlike the previous schemes, successful outputs occupy fixed modes and require no further conditional output routing. In particular, we show that the gate is more robust to heralded ancillary-photon loss than previously proposed boosted gates and reduces the average number of single photons required to generate a six-qubit ring graph state by more than $4.6\%$ compared with other type-I schemes. It therefore offers a resource-efficient primitive for scalable fusion-based photonic quantum information processing.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed type-I photonic fusion gate reaches 5/8 (62.5%) direct success using just two independent ancillary photons, matching a prior four-photon scheme with half the ancilla.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower ancillary-photon demand and fixed output modes could simplify resource-efficient photonic quantum computing hardware.
method: Use two independent single-photon ancillas without entangled ancillary input.
Combine predominantly passive optics with one detection-controlled phase-shift or mode-swap element.
Keep successful outputs in fixed modes, avoiding conditional output routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved robustness to heralded ancillary-photon loss and more than 4.6% lower average single-photon consumption for six-qubit ring graph generation versus other type-I schemes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract presents a proposed design rather than an experimental demonstration; detection-conditioned active control remains an implementation requirement.
infographic.paper_title: Minimal ancilla for boosting type-I photonic fusion

title: Feasibility of Distributed Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing: From Quantum Links to Algorithms
authors: Takumi Kobayashi, Hodaka Kurokawa, Yasunari Suzuki, Hideo Kosaka
abstract: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a large number of physical qubits, posing a major challenge for scaling up individual quantum processors. Distributed architectures offer a promising solution by interconnecting multiple processors through quantum networks. However, remote Bell-pair generation remains technically demanding, making it essential to assess computational performance under limited communication resources. In this work, we present a comprehensive resource analysis of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation using superconducting processors connected by microwave or optical links. We show that even a single physical communication channel per node can substantially reduce the physical-qubit requirements per node under experimentally motivated, forward-looking microwave-link assumptions of a 1 MHz physical Bell-pair generation rate and 90% fidelity, although at the cost of a roughly tenfold increase in execution time. Conversely, reducing the execution-time overhead requires substantially greater communication resources, including higher Bell-pair fidelities and extensive multiplexing. These results demonstrate the potential feasibility of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation with limited communication resources and provide a quantitative basis for balancing quantum-link performance, processor size, and execution time.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed fault-tolerant quantum computing can substantially reduce physical qubits per node with just one communication channel per node, but at roughly tenfold longer execution time under the studied assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis quantifies trade-offs among processor size, quantum-link performance, and runtime when scaling interconnected superconducting processors.
method: Analyze fault-tolerant computing resources for superconducting processors connected by microwave or optical links.
Assess computational performance under limited remote Bell-pair generation resources.
Evaluate trade-offs involving Bell-pair fidelity, generation rate, and communication multiplexing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The resource analysis finds substantial per-node qubit savings with one physical channel per node under forward-looking microwave-link assumptions of 1 MHz Bell-pair generation and 90% fidelity.
infographic.watch_item: These are resource-analysis results, not an experimental demonstration; reducing runtime overhead requires higher Bell-pair fidelity and extensive multiplexing.
infographic.paper_title: Feasibility of Distributed Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing: From Quantum Links to Algorithms

title: Quantum-Classical Framework for the Joint Optimization of Bidirectional EV Charging and Trip Assignment
authors: Mustafa Musab, Sebastian Schmitt, Markus Wappler, Jörg Lässig, Daniel Müssig
abstract: The integration of bidirectional (V2G) charging allows electric vehicle (EV) fleets to operate as distributed energy assets. However, the joint optimization of charging schedules and trip assignments is NP-hard. Moreover, bidirectional power flows create non-monotonic state-of-charge (SoC) dynamics that weaken standard dual-based Benders cuts. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical Benders decomposition framework. To overcome the qubit overhead associated with encoding feasibility cuts, we introduce logic-based conflict cuts, which require near-zero auxiliary qubits. Furthermore, we develop a sparse recursive SoC formulation that reduces the constraint-matrix density by a factor of T/3 in the horizon length T. We demonstrate that our framework recovers MILP-optimal solutions on benchmark instances with a low auxiliary-qubit budget, and, as a minimal proof of concept, we execute a small instance end-to-end on IBM quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid quantum-classical Benders framework jointly optimizes bidirectional EV charging and trip assignments while limiting auxiliary-qubit overhead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports EV fleet scheduling that coordinates transportation needs with vehicle-to-grid energy exchange.
method: Decompose the joint scheduling problem using hybrid quantum-classical Benders optimization.
Use logic-based conflict cuts requiring near-zero auxiliary qubits.
Apply a sparse recursive state-of-charge formulation to reduce constraint-matrix density by a factor of T/3.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework recovers MILP-optimal solutions on benchmark instances with a low auxiliary-qubit budget and runs a small instance end-to-end on IBM quantum hardware.
infographic.watch_item: The small hardware proof of concept does not establish quantum speedup or scalability to operational fleet sizes.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Classical Framework for the Joint Optimization of Bidirectional EV Charging and Trip Assignment

title: Initial-State Preparation for Strongly Correlated Molecules from Matrix Product States: Benchmarking and Environment-Aware Divide-and-Conquer Compilation
authors: Haiqi Liu, Longfei Chang, Zhendong Li, Wei-Hai Fang
abstract: Compiling classically optimized matrix product states (MPSs) into quantum circuits is a promising route to initial-state preparation for strongly correlated molecules, but the accuracy, gate cost, and classical scalability of existing MPS compilation methods have not been systematically assessed. Here, we benchmark representative analytical, variational, and hybrid MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated systems including hydrogen chains and iron-sulfur clusters. We compare state infidelity, CNOT gate count, classical runtime, and parallel scalability across different system sizes and bond dimensions. We also introduce a divide-and-conquer environment-aware compilation algorithm (DCE), which optimizes each local isometry approximation according to its contribution to the prepared-state fidelity. The results reveal complementary operating regimes: direct variational compilation methods are gate-efficient for some smaller molecular systems with $O(10)$ qubits and $O(10)$ bond dimensions or moderate accuracy targets with infidelity of order $10^{-1}$, whereas divide-and-conquer methods scale more favorably for larger systems and relatively higher bond dimensions of $O(10\text{-}10^2)$, particularly when target infidelities below $10^{-1}$ are required. Within the latter family, environment-aware optimization improves accuracy over unitary-distance-based compilation while retaining task-level parallelism. For the FeMo-cofactor (FeMoco), we find the DCE algorithm together with the MPS obtained in the entanglement-minimized orbitals (EMOs) provides a resource-efficient route to initial-state preparation. Our results provide practical guidance for selecting and developing MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated molecular simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Environment-aware divide-and-conquer compilation improves MPS state-preparation accuracy over unitary-distance-based compilation while preserving task-level parallelism.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing compilation methods by system size, MPS bond dimension, and target infidelity can improve resource efficiency when preparing strongly correlated molecular states.
method: Benchmark analytical, variational, and hybrid MPS-to-circuit compilation methods.
Optimize local isometry approximations according to their contribution to prepared-state fidelity.
Combine environment-aware compilation with entanglement-minimized orbitals for FeMoco.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on hydrogen chains and iron–sulfur clusters compare infidelity, CNOT count, classical runtime, and parallel scalability, finding complementary regimes for variational and divide-and-conquer methods.
infographic.watch_item: No single method dominates: resource efficiency depends on system size, bond dimension, orbital choice, and accuracy target.
infographic.paper_title: Initial-State Preparation for Strongly Correlated Molecules from Matrix Product States: Benchmarking and Environment-Aware Divide-and-Conquer Compilation

title: Basis-set error bounds for first-quantised quantum simulation of chemistry
authors: Dominic W. Berry, Arkin Tikku, Sophia Simon, Ryan Babbush
abstract: In quantum simulation of electronic structure it is often expected that the estimate of the ground energy converges to the continuum basis limit at a rate of $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for a basis of size $N$. This has been found in analytical and numerical studies, but without a rigorous treatment of the error in the quantities considered in quantum algorithms. Here we show the $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error for a wide range of cases needed for quantum simulation of chemistry. We show the error in the ground energy scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for plane-wave as well as spatial grid bases. For the spatial grid we consider both a periodic system and a non-periodic system with open boundaries. For time evolution, our bound on the error in the state itself is weaker than $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$, but we show that the error in observables scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1})$ in important cases. In particular, we may consider a smoothed observable that describes the position of particles. We show that this error scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-5/3}+tN^{-1})$ for time $t$, again both for plane-wave and spatial grid bases. For the non-periodic grid case we use a condition that the true evolution would not result in significant leakage past the boundaries, which introduces basis error unrelated to the resolution of the discretisation. We also show the error in the kinetic energy of a particle scales as $\mathcal O((t+\log N)/N)$ for the plane-wave and grid bases. Together, these results show that $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error holds for many of the relevant cases for quantum algorithms (with a trivial log factor for kinetic energy).

infographic.key_insight: Rigorous bounds establish O(N⁻¹) ground-energy basis error for plane-wave and spatial-grid quantum chemistry simulations, with comparable scaling for important observables.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These bounds help quantum algorithm designers choose basis sizes to meet energy and observable accuracy targets.
method: Bound ground-energy errors for plane-wave bases and spatial grids with periodic or open boundaries.
Analyze time-evolution errors in smoothed position observables and particle kinetic energy.
Separate open-boundary leakage error from discretization-resolution error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results give smoothed-position error O(N⁻⁵ᐟ³ + tN⁻¹) and kinetic-energy error O((t + log N)/N), where N is basis size and t is evolution time.
infographic.watch_item: Full-state evolution has a weaker error bound; open-boundary grids also require negligible leakage beyond the simulation domain.
infographic.paper_title: Basis-set error bounds for first-quantised quantum simulation of chemistry
